title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether deterministic verifier augmentation (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The preregistered primary estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) evaluated with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and a paired bootstrap 95% CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics to conserve model‑call budget (model_calls_used = 200 vs preregistered independent per‑arm maximum = 400). Observed (confirmatory set): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired counts n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). Result: estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, give an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and provide concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the reserved exploratory pool, and pilot checks) to make repeats informative.

sections.introduction:
LLM‑assisted translation of human intent into device configurations promises to reduce operator error and speed routine NetOps work, but incorrectly ordered or ill‑scoped device changes can cause outages or policy violations. A common mitigation strategy in the literature and in prototypes is tool‑augmentation: couple an LLM generator to deterministic validators, sandboxed replay engines, or constrained executors in a generate–validate–repair pipeline so generated proposals are checked before execution (Bilal et al., 2026; Okula, 2026). While prior work reports task‑dependent correctness gains from such pipelines, conclusions depend critically on evaluation semantics (how generations are sampled, whether repairs are applied, and validator fidelity).

We preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) to estimate whether adding a deterministic verifier reduces verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial prompt clusters. The preregistration specified a paired binary estimand, exact McNemar testing, bootstrap CIs, deterministic task generation, explicit contamination and exclusion rules, and a fixed model‑call budget. The executed run produced a reproducible ceiling outcome (every confirmatory episode scored SAFE), rendering the preregistered causal contrast mechanically untestable under the executed generation semantics. This paper therefore presents three artifact‑grounded contributions: (1) a complete, deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts; (2) a precise diagnosis—grounded in execution and analysis artifacts—explaining why the confirmatory test was non‑informative; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations to ensure informative repeats.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and prototype reports document rapid interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis and limited remediation) and argue for workflow‑centred, replayable evaluations rather than static QA metrics (Bilal et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024). Methodological proposals and experiments have demonstrated that generate–validate–refine and divide–verify–refine pipelines can reduce explicit constraint violations on curated tasks when the external verifier/simulator faithfully encodes domain constraints (Zhang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026). Research into guardrails, schema‑based tool interfaces, and secure orchestration emphasizes operational trade‑offs: stricter deterministic checks can lower acceptance of unsafe proposals but may raise false refusals or operator burden if validators are incomplete or conservative (Ando, 2026; Okula, 2026).

The closest methodological guidance to our experiment stresses (a) explicit initial and final state task specifications, (b) deterministic topology/task generators, (c) sandbox replay and archived validator traces for reproducibility, and (d) adversarial or red‑teaming components to exercise guardrails before confirmatory testing (Ferrag et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025). Our design adopted these desiderata and preregistered both confirmatory and exploratory items so that ROC‑style diagnostics and refusal‑rate trade‑offs could be estimated when the exploratory reserve was consumed.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered as cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded − baseline) on binary SAFE indicators produced by a deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar; confidence intervals: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). Planned paired tasks: N = 200; planned paired episodes = 400.

Task generator, scope, and seeds. A deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to single‑AS multi‑device topologies and limited fields (admin, mtu, vlan). Each task manifest contained initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, difficulty metadata, and a generation_seed. The preregistration included an adversarial transform rule set and reserved up to 50 exploratory tasks to calibrate adversarial strength before confirmatory execution.

Pipelines compared and scoring. Baseline pipeline: accept the LLM candidate and score post hoc with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded pipeline: validate the candidate in a deterministic sandbox using deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the validator emitted structured traces and a deterministic binary valid flag (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). In the confirmatory episodes no automatic repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace fields are null), so guarded outcomes reflect validation only. All scoring used the scorer rule full_intent_constraint_validation.

Generation semantics, model, and budgeting. The preregistration permitted two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (one model call per arm per task → ~400 calls) or shared_initial_candidate (one model call per task shared across arms → 200 calls). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate to conserve the hosted model budget. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Executed accounting: model_calls_used = 200 (execution manifest).

Analysis pipeline and determinism checks. Confirmatory binary outcomes were derived from validator.valid and analyzed with paired_binary_analysis_v1 to compute the 2×2 contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Preregistered missingness/exclusion rules (one automatic retry per failed model call; exclude nondeterministic verifier tasks) were applied automatically; deterministic reconciliation and provider audit checks were recorded.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic audit. The archived execution manifest reports completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200, consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics. Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200; no cross‑condition cache reuse was observed. Deterministic reconciliation checks passed and no technical exclusions or nondeterministic verifier behaviours were recorded.

Primary confirmatory contingency and statistics. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory candidate as SAFE: baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200. Paired contingency counts: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. From these counts the estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). These values match the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv).

Representative diagnostic traces. Representative scoring JSONs and validator traces show identical raw generated candidates used by both arms and validator.validation_after.valid = true with violation_count = 0. repair_provider_trace fields are null in the confirmatory scoring JSONs, confirming no repairs were invoked. Because the same candidate was shared across arms and validators agreed on validity for every task, there were no discordant pairs that McNemar’s test requires for inference about the paired effect.

Missingness, exploratory reserves, and inferential consequence. The analysis/missingness_summary documents complete_pairs = 200; no exploratory reserve items were consumed before confirmatory execution. The degenerate contingency (all SAFE) makes the preregistered confirmatory test non‑informative for the causal question of whether deterministic validator augmentation reduces unsafe proposals in this setting: when n10 = n01 = 0 the paired test returns p = 1.0 and a degenerate CI at zero, which reflects absence of arm‑level variation under the executed semantics rather than demonstrated equivalence of strategies.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded diagnosis. Three archived facts together explain the non‑informative outcome: (1) generation semantics — the run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one LLM candidate per task scored by both arms; (2) validator outcomes — deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled each candidate SAFE (baseline SAFE = 200/200); and (3) no repairs applied — repair traces are null. These archived facts (execution/model_configuration.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) imply the arms had no opportunity to disagree, so the paired causal contrast could not produce informative discordance.

Design lessons and concrete recommendations (artifact‑supported). All recommendations follow directly from preregistered artifacts and executed accounting:
- Use independent per‑arm generation when the estimand is a paired causal contrast attributable to the presence of a verifier; for N=200 this requires ≈400 total model calls instead of the 200 used here. This arithmetic is explicit in the preregistration execution_contract and the execution manifest.
- Before confirmatory runs, consume the preregistered exploratory reserve (we reserved up to 50 tasks) to calibrate adversarial transforms until the baseline unsafe rate matches power assumptions; archive these calibration runs and freeze parameters in the preregistration to preserve confirmatory validity.
- Instrument and archive repair traces when repairs are permitted; quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions and check for repair‑induced violations. In our run repair traces are null and therefore did not provide a mechanism for inducing discordance.
- Perform a deterministic pilot check on a small holdout prior to the full confirmatory run; if the pilot yields a ceiling/floor contingency (no discordant pairs), abort and follow preregistered contingency‑preserving paths (enable independent per‑arm draws or strengthen adversarial transforms) rather than proceeding to a confirmatory test that will be uninformative.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the principal internal threat here is generation semantics sensitivity — shared generation eliminated per‑arm variation. Construct validity: the binary validator.valid captures a specific set of intent→configuration constraints (admin/mtu/vlan patterns and required_sequence); it may not capture broader operational failure modes. External validity: tasks were synthetic, single‑AS, and limited in scope; only one model (gpt-5-mini) and one deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were evaluated. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power plan assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate (≈10–15%); that assumption failed here, invalidating the planned power calculation for the executed semantics.

Operational implications. The archived artifacts quantify the resource trade‑off between independent per‑arm generation and shared generation, making explicit the model‑call cost of testing paired causal contrasts. Teams must weigh additional model calls and exploratory calibration cost against the risk of non‑informative confirmatory runs. For deployment, validators must be validated against broader operational rule sets and human adjudication should be considered when validators are incomplete.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt-5-mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the declared model and validator, both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this run. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) we publish a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts that permit exact replay; (2) we provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) we give concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the exploratory reserve, and pilot checks) for informative repeats. The archived execution and analysis artifacts cited throughout permit deterministic replication of the diagnosis and should be consulted prior to repeats or deployment extrapolation.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
